power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps > .106", Text = "Across all seeds and modalities, the models did not predict participants' BED status above chance (all ps > .106, Fig. 2; See Fig. S2 for ACC results)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Binge eating disorder (BED) is associated with obesity as well as behavioral and neurobiological changes in the reward and cognitive control systems of the brain.
To better dissociate neural mechanisms of pathological eating behavior, functional connectivity (FC) analyses have shown promise.
However, there is currently no replicable signature of BED derived from fMRI.
We investigated FC in 61 women with varying symptoms of binge eating.
The three groups included 21 women with BED, 20 women with subsyndromal BED (subBED), and 20 controls without binge eating (noBE) matched in body mass index (BMI) and age.

To identify neural signatures of BED and BMI, we used seed-based FC "fingerprints" (nucleus accumbens, NAcc, for reward and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dlPFC, for cognitive control) to predict group or BMI based on resting state and taskbased (food bidding) FC.
Furthermore, we explored spatial patterns of FC to quantify associations with BED and BMI.
Both seeds of the reward and cognitive control networks robustly predicted BMI (rs = .33 -.46).
The dlPFC seed predicted BMI across conditions (resting state: p=.002; task: p=.012) while the NAcc seed only predicted BMI based on task-based FC (p=.007).
In contrast, FC failed to classify binge eating groups better than chance.
FC within reward and cognitive control networks primarily reflect obesity-related changes.
Despite pronounced differences in eating behavior, BED could not be reliably dissociated from subBED or noBE using FC fingerprints.
These results highlight challenges in identifying BED-specific functional markers.
Binge eating disorder (BED) is the most prevalent eating disorder (1) with a lifetime prevalence of 0.6-1.8% in women and 0.3-0.7% in men (2).

text.text: Often, neuroimaging studies investigating obesity do not control for binge eating symptoms, potentially conflating associations of body weight with pathological eating (30, 31).

text.text: Since BED is strongly associated with obesity, it is still unclear whether differences in brain function are largely driven by obesity or if specific signatures indicative of pathological eating can be isolated.

To address this gap and disentangle shared and distinct FC alterations between BED and obesity, we examined FC in a sample of 61 overweight or obese women, including 21 individuals diagnosed with BED, 20 individuals exhibiting current binge eating behavior without meeting the diagnosis criteria for BED (i.e., subsyndromal BED, subBED), and 20 weight-matched controls without binge eating (noBE).

Crucially, we investigated both resting state and task-based FC during a food bidding task, capitalizing on FC in response to relevant stimuli, which has been suggested to improve brain-behavior associations (32).

text.text: To capture the functional relevance of reward and cognitive control processes, we used . seed-to-ROI (whole brain) FC profiles from the NAcc and dlPFC to predict BED and BMI.
In total, 61 females divided into three groups participated in the study (Mage = 39.7 years ± 13.2, range 21 and 64 years; MBMI = 31.5 kg/m 2 ± 7.1).
The first group included individuals diagnosed with BED.

The second group were classified as subBED because they reported objective binge-eating episodes during the preceding 12 months but failed to meet the frequency criterion for a diagnosis of BED, met only two instead of three out of five existing criteria for an objective binge, or lacked marked distress regarding binge eating.
The third group of participants reported having no lifetime history of subjective and objective binge eating or other eating disorders (noBE).
The noBE group was matched to participants with BED according to age and BMI.

text.text: Food items were presented in 12 blocks (5 images per block) of four categories (high-calorie savory, high-calorie sweet, low-calorie savory, low-calorie sweet), and images were shown twice.
Prior to each block, a fixation cross was displayed.
At the end of the cue reactivity phase, participants were asked to indicate how much physical effort they were willing to exert to gain access to a buffet including the items shown previously.
By pressing the grip force device, a blue ball shown in a vertical tube on the screen could be lifted, with the height of the ball being proportional to the force participants applied.
The force was determined relative to each participant's maximum force that had previously been recorded in a training phase of an effort allocation task (41, 43, 44).

To evaluate the discriminative capacity of FCs among distinct BED groups, we used a multiclass classification approach.
The classification model consisted of a one-versus-all 3-class error-correcting output codes (ECOC) model with ensembles of decision trees as binary learners (100 ensemble learning cycles).

text.text: We next examined whether FC patterns were associated with participants' BMI.
Using seed-to-ROI FC from the resting state and task conditions, elastic net regression models significantly predicted BMI for multiple seeds.
In the task condition, FC patterns of all ROIs predicted BMI (NAcc: p = 0.007, R² = 0.199; dlPFC: p = 0.012, R² = 0.166; ACC: p = 0.001, R² = 0.258).
Statistical significance was determined using permutation tests (1,000 iterations) with a baseline model that included age and BED groups as confounders.

In contrast, resting state FC was only predictive of BMI from the dlPFC seed (p = 0.002, R² = 0.243), while NAcc and ACC FC did not predict BMI (p = 0.69, R² = -0.029; and p = .67, R² = -.022, respectively; Fig. 4 and SI).

text.text: To determine which connectivity patterns contributed to the significant BMI prediction, we examined the standardized elastic net regression coefficients, or βweights, from the seed-to-ROI models that predicted BMI: task-based NAcc-to-ROI, resting-state dlPFC-to-ROI, and task-based dlPFC-to-ROI connectivity.

Regarding the NAcc seed, frontal and dorsal striatum regions were among the strongest contributors to the BMI prediction, although with mixed signs (higher connectivity with the putamen and lower connectivity with the caudate).

Other contributions were observed for subcortical regions implicated in homeostatic and autonomic regulation, including higher hypothalamic connectivity and decreased connectivity with the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and brainstem.

For the dlPFC models, connectivity with the caudate contributed positively to BMI prediction in both resting-state and task conditions, together with frontal cortical regions, including the inferior frontal gyrus (Figure 5).

text.text: Finally, to assess whether task-and resting-state FC captured similar or differential spatial patterns, we compared the standardized elastic net weights of ROIs selected in at least one of the modalities for the dlPFC seed.
The task-based and resting state weight patterns showed a weak to moderate correspondence (median Pearson r = .18 and Spearman ρ = .39; Figure S6), with 14 predictors shared between the two models.

text.text: Of these shared predictors, 92.9% showed weights in the same direction.
These findings suggest that task-and resting-state dlPFC FC capture relatively distinct predictive patterns.
BED frequently co-occurs with obesity (35) and has been associated with altered function in brain systems supporting reward processing and cognitive control (16, 17).

text.text: However, disentangling neural mechanisms related to pathological eating behavior from those associated with obesity remains a major challenge.
To this end, FC analyses have been proposed as a promising approach.
Yet a robust and replicable fMRI-based neural signature of BED has not been established to date.
Using . multivariate approaches, we examined FC patterns derived from a priori seed regions during resting state and task fMRI.
FC patterns reliably predicted BMI beyond chance, whereas binge eating status could not be predicted using either resting state or taskbased FC.

Among the examined seed regions, dlPFC connectivity emerged as the most robust predictor of BMI across brain states, while predictive effects of NAcc and ACC connectivity were primarily observed during task performance.
Together, these findings suggest that alterations in cognitive control and reward networks are more closely related to obesity than binge eating behavior.
Contrary to our expectations, we found no reliable neural signature of binge eating behavior.

Neither multivariate classification analyses nor mass-univariate comparisons of FC maps revealed significant differences between individuals with binge eating behavior and individuals without any history of binge eating.
These findings contrast with previous work reporting altered frontostriatal FC in BED.

For example, Haynos et al. (21) observed reduced resting state FC between the NAcc and frontal as well as posterior cingulate regions, which was associated with impaired reversal learning and increased binge eating frequency.

text.text: Here, we were unable to replicate these findings.
Instead, an ROI-based analysis suggested a numerically stronger FC among individuals with binge eating behavior in our sample.
Differences in sample characteristics, preprocessing choices, or statistical thresholds may partly account for these discrepancies (59).
text.formatted: Differences in sample characteristics, preprocessing choices, or statistical thresholds may partly account for these discrepancies <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(59)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, both studies were characterized by modest sample sizes, which may limit reproducibility and increase sensitivity to sampling variability (60).
text.formatted: In addition, both studies were characterized by modest sample sizes, which may limit reproducibility and increase sensitivity to sampling variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(60)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of statistically significant group differences does not preclude the existence of BED-specific alterations in FC.

Instead, our findings suggest that potential BED-related FC differences are smaller than anticipated and potentially context-dependent or overshadowed by obesity-related alterations in brain function.
In contrast to binge eating status, BMI could be reliably predicted from FC patterns within cognitive control and reward networks.
Among the examined regions, the dlPFC showed the strongest and most consistent predictive value across both resting state and task conditions.

As a central node of the frontoparietal control network, the dlPFC is critically involved in executive functions such as inhibitory control (61), self-regulation (62), and the modulation of food craving (63, 64).
text.formatted: As a central node of the frontoparietal control network, the dlPFC is critically involved in executive functions such as inhibitory control (61), self-regulation (62), and the modulation of food craving <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(63,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64)</ref>.

text.text: The importance of the dlPFC for regulating eating behavior is further supported by preclinical work showing that prefrontal projections to the hypothalamus orchestrate cue-potentiated . food intake (65).
text.formatted: The importance of the dlPFC for regulating eating behavior is further supported by preclinical work showing that prefrontal projections to the hypothalamus orchestrate cue-potentiated . food intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(65)</ref>.

text.text: In humans, stimulation of the dlPFC has been shown to reduce food craving (66).
text.formatted: In humans, stimulation of the dlPFC has been shown to reduce food craving <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(66)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this regulatory role, previous studies have often reported reduced dlPFC connectivity in obesity, particularly within frontoparietal networks (24) and lower global brain connectivity (67).
text.formatted: In line with this regulatory role, previous studies have often reported reduced dlPFC connectivity in obesity, particularly within frontoparietal networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> and lower global brain connectivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(67)</ref>.

text.text: At the other end of the spectrum, anorexia nervosa, which is characterized by excessive cognitive control over food intake, has been associated with increased dlPFC recruitment (68, 69).
text.formatted: At the other end of the spectrum, anorexia nervosa, which is characterized by excessive cognitive control over food intake, has been associated with increased dlPFC recruitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(68,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">69)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to reduced FC to some brain regions (e.g., putamen and pallidum), we also observed that BMI prediction was driven by increased FC between the dlPFC and other regions of the motivational circuit, such as the ACC and the (70, 71) whereas decreases have been shown in anorexia nervosa (72) and bulimia nervosa (73).
text.formatted: In addition to reduced FC to some brain regions (e.g., putamen and pallidum), we also observed that BMI prediction was driven by increased FC between the dlPFC and other regions of the motivational circuit, such as the ACC and the (70, 71) whereas decreases have been shown in anorexia nervosa <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(72)</ref> and bulimia nervosa <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(73)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that obesityrelated alterations in dlPFC connectivity may not reflect a uniform reduction, but rather a more specific reorganization of network interactions.

Guo et al. (74) recently reported increased variability of FC between the limbic and frontoparietal networks in individuals with higher BMI, suggesting greater fluctuations in the functional coupling between networks involved in reward processing and cognitive control.

text.text: Increased connectivity may reflect compensatory processes or reduced neural efficiency, indicating that greater neural resources are required to maintain cognitive control in individuals with higher BMI.
Task-based connectivity further enhanced BMI prediction for reward-and control-related regions.
While dlPFC FC predicted BMI in both brain states, predictive effects of ACC and NAcc FC emerged primarily during task performance.
Participants completed a food-bidding task involving food cues (75) that reliably engage reward and cognitive control systems (76).
text.formatted: Participants completed a food-bidding task involving food cues (75) that reliably engage reward and cognitive control systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(76)</ref>.

text.text: Task states have been shown to enhance individual FC signatures (77) by increasing the ratio of within-subject to between-subject variability (32, 78).
text.formatted: Task states have been shown to enhance individual FC signatures (77) by increasing the ratio of within-subject to between-subject variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">78)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this notion, food-related cognitive and motivational engagement during the task may have amplified obesity-related FC differences within reward and control networks (79).
text.formatted: In line with this notion, food-related cognitive and motivational engagement during the task may have amplified obesity-related FC differences within reward and control networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(79)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the slightly reduced predictive strength of dlPFC FC during task performance may indicate that cognitive engagement partially compensates for intrinsic control deficits that are more apparent during resting state conditions.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings.
First, the fMRI sample consisted only of women, reflecting the higher prevalence of BED in women (2).
In addition, binge eating is influenced by ovarian hormones (80), and future studies may account for menstrual cycle phase or hormone levels.
text.formatted: In addition, binge eating is influenced by ovarian hormones <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(80)</ref>, and future studies may account for menstrual cycle phase or hormone levels.

text.text: Second, . although comparable to many fMRI studies in the field, the sample size limits the robustness and generalizability of predictive modeling approaches.
Larger datasets will be necessary to improve statistical power and model stability.
Third, compared to the online assessment, the BMI range in our sample was limited by scanner constraints, restricting coverage of severe obesity.
Finally, the cross-sectional design precludes causal conclusions about whether FC alterations precede or result from weight gain.
In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that FC within reward and cognitive control networks appears to vary primarily as a function of obesity rather than binge eating behavior in women.
While BMI could be reliably predicted from FC patterns, we found no robust neural signature of binge eating behavior.

These findings highlight the substantial overlap between obesity and binge eating behavior at the neural level and underscore the challenge of disentangling disorder-specific effects from obesity-related alterations.

Future studies should therefore employ larger samples, longitudinal designs, and multiple brain states to better characterize individual variability in reward and cognitive control networks and to clarify their role in the development of obesity and disordered eating.

Figure 1: Overview of experimental tasks and connectivity regions of interest. a) Illustration of the food bidding task performed in the scanner.
Each block starts with 4 s presentation of each picture for that block.
Then, after a fixation cross is shown for 4 s (jittered), participants indicate their willingness to work for the presented food by pressing a grip force device during 5 s.
The height of a blue ball inside a vertical tube depicted on the screen represents the force applied by the participants relative to their maximum force. b) Snapshot from Inscapes.
Inscapes is a computer-generated animation with a fixed camera angle and no scene cuts that was shown during acquisition of resting state data (40). c) FC seeds and regions of interest (ROIs).
The NAcc seed was defined using the Harvard-Oxford atlas.
As there are no specific dlPFC parcellations in said atlas, we used the regions corresponding to the middle frontal gyrus (midFG).
The lower right panel shows the ROIs reported by Haynos et al. (2021) that showed lower NAcc connectivity in BED vs. control groups.
These ROIs were generated to replicate seed-based NAcc differences.
Figure 2.
BED status cannot be classified better than chance based on seed-to-ROI FC for resting state and task fMRI.
NAcc-to-ROI and dlPFC-to-ROI classification accuracy are shown for resting state and task conditions.
For each seed and condition, a multiclass confusion matrix shows the normalized proportion of participants in each observed group (columns) classified into each predicted group (rows).
Additionally, the distribution of the classification accuracy generated by permutation testing is shown, with a red vertical line representing the observed data test statistic.
The median accuracy of the permutation test was used as a comparison baseline (1,000 iterations).
Figure 3.
No significant differences in functional connectivity (FC) between NAcc and previously reported regions differenciating BED and control groups by Haynos et al.
The NAcc FC is depicted for each ROI and BED status group.
Small data points represent the mean FC per ROI of individual participants.
Large points represent the mean FC for each group and the error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).
Figure 4.
BMI can be successfully predicted based on seed-to-ROI FC for resting state and task fMRI.
NAcc-to-ROI and dlPFC-to-ROI prediction accuracy are shown for resting state and task conditions.
For each seed and condition, a scatter plot displays the relationship between observed BMI and predicted BMI, with fitted regression lines and shaded 95% confidence intervals.

Additionally, a distribution of the coefficient of determination (R² measure of goodness of fit) generated by permutation testing is shown, with the vertical red line representing the observed test statistic (1,000 iterations).
For visualization, the permutation-derived R² values were centered by subtracting the median of the null distribution, such that zero corresponds to the median permutation performance.
Negative values indicate prediction performance below the median of the null distribution, and positive values indicate prediction performance above the median of the null distribution.
Figure 5.
BMI prediction is supported by increased frontal, striatal, and somatomotor connectivity.
Standardized β-weights for FC features retained in at least 80% of cross-validation iterations are shown for each seed region and condition.
Positive weight values (warm colors) indicate features contributing positively to BMI prediction, whereas negative weight values (cold colors) indicate features contributing negatively.
Across models, the strongest positive weights were predominantly observed within frontal and dorsal striatal, and somatomotor regions, with additional cerebellar, and subcortical structures.
Seed regions were excluded from their respective predictor sets.
